query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In an initially single-phase equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy with coarse grains (~50 µm), intermediate-temperature tensile deformation (e.g., at ~650°C) induces rapid nanosegregation of principal elements (notably Ni, Cr, and Mn) to the grain boundaries, which reduces interfacial cohesion and triggers a transition from transgranular ductile fracture to brittle intergranular cracking. However, if a controlled heat-treatment is applied to induce preexisting Cr-rich precipitates at the grain boundaries, these precipitates will preferentially capture the segregating embrittling elements, thereby maintaining higher ductility under identical conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast single-phase equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi HEA with coarse grains (~50 µm) and no engineered secondary phases.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled heat treatment to one set of samples to precipitate Cr-rich secondary phases at the grain boundaries while leaving a reference set in the as-cast single-phase condition. Then, subject both sets to tensile loading at an intermediate temperature (around 650°C) at controlled strain rates.
generation.conditions: Tensile testing at ~650°C under similar strain rate conditions, chosen based on previous studies of intermediate-temperature ductility loss.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoclusters of segregated principal elements forming along grain boundaries, with their density modulated by the presence or absence of preexisting Cr-rich precipitates.
generation.mechanism: In the as-cast single-phase alloy, thermally activated deformation at 650°C causes fast segregation (nanoclustering) of Ni, Cr, and Mn to the GBs, which weakens grain-boundary cohesion and promotes intergranular brittle fracture. The engineered introduction of Cr-rich precipitates acts as a sink for these embrittling species, relieving their accumulation at GBs, thereby preserving ductility by maintaining higher intergranular cohesion.
generation.predicted_outcome: The as-cast single-phase HEA will exhibit a notable drop in ductility with brittle, intergranular fracture surfaces (e.g., a significant reduction in elongation compared to room temperature values), whereas the heat-treated alloy with engineered GB precipitates will retain considerably higher ductility and display more ductile (transgranular) fracture features. The improvement could be on the order of several-fold increased fracture strain relative to the baseline.
generation.baseline: The mechanical behavior of the as-cast single-phase CrMnFeCoNi HEA under intermediate-temperature tensile testing, which shows ductility loss due to GB nanosegregation-induced decohesion.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected to be most pronounced at intermediate temperatures (approximately 600–700°C) and under strain rates where thermally activated segregation processes compete with deformation. At much lower temperatures or extremely high strain rates, the segregation kinetics may not lead to significant GB decohesion.
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of nanosegregation, the critical concentration of segregated elements required to trigger GB decohesion, and the stability and distribution of the engineered Cr-rich precipitates may introduce variability. There is also uncertainty regarding the interplay between dislocation activity and GB segregation at different strains.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CrMnFeCoNi HEA samples: one set in the as-cast single-phase state and another set subjected to a controlled heat treatment to form preexisting Cr-rich precipitates along the grain boundaries. Conduct tensile tests at 650°C under identical strain rate conditions. In parallel, perform atom probe tomography or high-resolution TEM on the grain boundaries of deformed samples to quantify element segregation.
measurements: Tensile stress-elongation curves (measuring yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation to failure)
Fractography (SEM/TEM) to identify intergranular vs. transgranular fracture modes
Grain boundary chemical composition analysis via atom probe tomography or energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both the as-cast and heat-treated samples exhibit indistinguishable ductility loss and similar GB elemental segregation profiles (i.e., if engineered precipitates fail to capture segregating elements and do not alter fracture mode), then the hypothesis that GB nanosegregation-induced decohesion is mitigated by preexisting precipitates is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The presence of intermetallic compounds, such as brittle Laves phases, typically reduces the ductility of RHEAs (), prompting extensive efforts to develop single-phase RHEAs for high-temperature applications (, , , , , , ). The equiatomic Ti-V-Nb-Ta alloy is one of the most attractive RHEAs, which solidifies as a single-phase body-centered cubic (BCC) microstructure with heterogeneous elemental distribution and exhibits excellent high-temperature strength and room-temperature ductility (). Equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta has an extremely high compressive yield strength, 1273 MPa at room temperature and 688 MPa at 900°C (). By comparison, conventional high-temperature Ni-base superalloys notably soften above 600°C, with the compressive yield strength dropping to ~200 MPa at 900°C (). Equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta also exhibits impressive tensile ductility, ~14% at room temperature (), and a relatively low brittle-to-ductile transition temperature between −47° and −27°C, comparable to BCC metals and stainless steels for engineering applications (, ). During the tensile test process at intermediate temperatures in the air, intermetallic phases were not yet formed in coarse-grained Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni HEAs, owing to a short testing time (a few minutes). In addition, the above-mentioned oxide and hydrogen embrittlement mechanisms can be ruled out because these alloys show good resistance to oxidation at intermediate temperatures and hydrogen embrittlement at relatively low hydrogen concentrations (, ). These facts suggest that temperature-induced ductility loss in fcc-phase HEAs/MEAs could be related to segregation of some of the principal elements during the short testing time, which causes GB decohesion. We examined this hypothesis in an equiatomic Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEA and revealed the fast segregation of Cr, Mn, and Ni separately into GBs, which accounts for ductility loss with increasing temperature. Correspondingly, we proposed and demonstrated that preexisting precipitates can migrate the fast segregation of Cr, Mn, and Ni into the precipitates instead of at GBs, which can effectively evade ductility loss during deformation at intermediate temperatures.

In addition, the segregation of trace elements C and B into GBs is beneficial to improve GB cohesion as long as M6C carbides do not precipitate (, ). The 1D compositional profiles in fig. S4 show that the C and B composition at Cr-enriched and Ni(Mn)-enriched GBs is very low, which is insufficient to form carbides or borides at GBs. A recent study of the single-phase fcc CoFeNi2V0.5Mo0.2 HEA demonstrated that the lack of Cr and Mn can evade ductility loss at intermediate temperatures (). Therefore, we believe that the segregation of Cr, Ni, and Mn at GBs in Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni system HEAs can embrittle GBs and, hence, lead to ductility loss with increasing deformation temperature. Note that the segregation of Cr, Ni, and Mn at GBs also occurs at relatively low temperatures (<700°C), which accounts for ductility loss at intermediate temperatures. In the current work, the sample after tensile test at 700°C, exhibiting remarkable ductility loss though maintaining a strain hardening capacity, provides a good model example to demonstrate our hypothesis: Nanoclustering induced GB embrittlement in HEAs at intermediate temperatures. cited_evidence.text: Segregation of minor alloying elements to GBs often embrittles conventional alloys (, ). Grain refinement is an effective way to evade GB embrittlement because more interfaces reduce the level of individual GB segregation (). In contrast, multiple principal constitutive elements in HEAs can segregate into GBs instead of trace alloying elements. In HEAs, grain refinement can assist the segregation of principal constitutive elements to GBs and even lead to the formation of brittle intermetallic phases at GBs (). For example, Cr-rich bcc phases and L10-NiMn phases precipitate at GBs in nanocrystalline Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEA (grain size, ~50 nm) after annealing at 450°C for only 5 min, which reduces the ductility substantially (). In addition, previous studies show that Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEAs with the grain sizes from 4.4 to 155 μm all exhibit loss of ductility at intermediate temperatures, irrespective of grain size in this range (Fig. 1). Microalloying with B in Fe-Mn steels has been reported to delay temper embrittlement at 450°C (). B can compete for GB sites and reduce GB energy and, thus, repel the embrittling element Mn due to the decreased driving force for Mn segregation

Both HT-1 and HT-2 samples have almost identical tensile strength and ductility at 25°C (Table 1 and Figure 6); ductile transgranular fractures were dominant at room temperature (Figure 7(a,c)). However, when testing temperature was increased to 650°C, a significant hot ductility drop was observed for HT-1 sample. According to Figure 7(b), the facet cleavage surface and the limited amount of plastic deformation indicate that the failure mechanism was brittle intergranular fracture. The brittleness of HT-1 sample was even more pronounced under creep at 650°C as the creep fracture strain was only 0.03%. Cleavage edges on crept fracture surface (Figure 9(b)) and crack propagation along straight grain boundary (Figure 10(b)) indicate the vulnerability of straight grain boundary in HT-1 samples at elevated temperature. According to the local strain concentration at triple junctions of grain boundaries (Figure 11(a)), it is probable that HT-1 samples encountered an embrittlement at 650°C. The initiation of creep damage of HT-1 sample was a result of vacancy coalescence on grain boundaries perpendicular to the loading direction and severe strain concentration at grain boundaries. papers.title: Origin of age softening in the refractory high-entropy alloys.
papers.approach: Combined advanced analytical microscopy, CALPHAD modeling, and nanoindentation to study aging at high temperature (700°C) and impurity effects.
papers.findings: Aging promotes phase segregation driven by trace interstitials (oxygen, nitrogen) that initially contribute to solid-solution strengthening. Their depletion in regions near grain boundaries generates compositionally distinct zones (PFZs) linked to progressive softening.
papers.mechanism: Impurity-assisted nanoscale phase segregation depletes the solute interstitial strengthening effect near grain boundaries, potentially preconditioning the alloy for later loss in toughness if similar compositional gradients occur.

papers.title: Grain boundary decohesion by nanoclustering Ni and Cr separately in CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloys.
papers.system: CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (single-phase fcc solid solution)
papers.approach: Microstructural analysis (including atom probe tomography, TEM, and STEM) combined with mechanical testing at intermediate temperatures; comparison between single‐phase and dual‐phase (via pre‐existing Cr-rich precipitates) samples.
papers.findings: At intermediate temperatures, fast segregation and nanoclustering of principal elements (Ni, Cr, and Mn) occur at grain boundaries, leading to intergranular fracture and ductility loss in the single-phase alloy. In contrast, when embrittling elements are captured in preexisting precipitates, ductility is retained.
papers.mechanism: Nanoclustering-induced grain boundary decohesion reduces cohesion along the interfaces and triggers brittleness, even in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy.

papers.title: Effect of serrated grain boundary on tensile and creep properties of a precipitation strengthened high entropy alloy.
papers.system: Precipitation-strengthened high-entropy alloy (HT-1 vs. HT-2 samples with different GB morphologies)
papers.approach: Tensile and creep testing at room temperature and 650°C combined with detailed microstructural analysis comparing straight versus serrated grain boundary morphologies.
papers.findings: Samples with straight grain boundaries exhibit a dramatic loss of ductility (brittle intergranular failure) at elevated temperatures, while serrated grain boundaries distribute local strains more evenly and enhance ductility and creep life by factors of up to 3.5 and 400, respectively.
papers.mechanism: Grain boundary serration reduces strain concentration and suppresses intergranular crack initiation; conversely, smooth GBs provide preferential paths for brittle failure, suggesting that GB morphology strongly modulates toughness degradation.

papers.title: Mitigating Strain Localization via Stabilized Phase Boundaries for Strengthening Multi-Principal Element Alloys.
papers.system: Multi-principal element alloys with engineered nanoscale phase boundaries (BCC and FCC phases)
papers.approach: Introduction of heterogeneous, yet coherent, phase boundaries inspired by natural microstructures (e.g., mouse enamel) to provide channels for dislocation transfer while mitigating strain localization, without additional heat treatment.
papers.findings: The alloy achieved ultra-high tensile strength and ductility, suggesting that controlled phase-boundary structures can arrest localized deformation that would otherwise lead to premature brittle behavior.
papers.mechanism: Stabilized phase boundaries act as effective barriers to strain localization and cracks by harmonizing traditional toughening mechanisms (crack deflection, blocking, bridging) at the microstructural level.

established: In conventional alloys, grain-boundary segregation (of impurities or secondary phases) leads to brittle behavior via loss of cohesion at interfaces.
High-entropy alloys, despite being compositionally complex and initially single-phase, can also suffer toughness degradation at intermediate temperatures due to nanoscale segregation phenomena.
Microstructural features such as grain boundary morphology (e.g., serration) play a pivotal role in mitigating or exacerbating brittle intergranular failure.

approaches_tried.approach: GB segregation engineering by inducing preexisting embrittling element–rich precipitates
approaches_tried.outcome: Successfully mitigated ductility loss at intermediate temperatures by capturing segregating elements, as evidenced in dual-phase Cr-rich σ phase alloys.

approaches_tried.approach: Modifying grain boundary morphology (from straight to serrated) via tailored heat treatments
approaches_tried.outcome: Dramatically enhanced high-temperature ductility and creep life by reducing local strain concentrations.

mechanisms: Nanoclustering of principal elements (Ni, Cr, Mn) at grain boundaries reduces grain boundary cohesion (GB decohesion), leading to intergranular cracking and brittle behavior.
Impurity-induced phase segregation depletes strengthening interstitials near GBs, promoting local softening that may predispose the alloy to brittleness.
Grain boundary morphology (e.g., serration) can modulate local strain distribution and delay or prevent crack initiation.
Stabilized, coherent phase boundaries can distribute dislocation activity to avoid strain localization and subsequent brittle fracture.
disagreements: While conventional alloy theory predicts that single-phase solid solutions should avoid brittle intergranular embrittlement, experimental evidence in high-entropy alloys indicates that even in the absence of classic intermetallic precipitation, nanosegregation of principal elements can trigger toughness degradation.

There is debate regarding whether precipitation per se is required for embrittlement or whether subtle compositional variations at GBs in seemingly homogeneous HEAs are sufficient to cause a brittle-to-ductile transition.
open_questions: What specific thermomechanical conditions (temperature, strain rate, aging time) trigger fast nanosegregation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy?
How does the inherent compositional complexity govern the kinetics and extent of grain boundary segregation compared to conventional alloys?
What are the precise limits (in terms of service conditions) at which GB decohesion transitions from a manageable ductile response to catastrophic brittle failure?
Can precise, controlled modification of GB morphology or engineered precipitate distribution provide predictable mitigation of brittleness?
opportunities: Perform a controlled comparison between an initially single-phase HEA subjected to service-simulating thermal and mechanical conditions versus an identical alloy with engineered GB segregation (e.g., via preexisting Cr-rich precipitates or induced serration) to directly test the role of nanosegregation in toughness degradation.
Combine in-situ high-resolution microscopy with mechanical testing at intermediate temperatures to dynamically monitor GB composition and validate the nanoclustering-induced decohesion hypothesis.

Explore the compositional space further by tuning the partitioning behavior of principal elements (or adding minor elements that inhibit segregation) to design alloys inherently resistant to brittle behavior.
Develop predictive models that couple thermodynamic calculations with kinetic segregation phenomena to forecast the onset of brittle behavior in service conditions.

directions.direction: Investigate the kinetics and extent of nanosegregation of principal elements (e.g., Ni, Cr, Mn) to grain boundaries during intermediate‐temperature tensile deformation using in‐situ microscopy and atom probe tomography.
directions.assessment: This approach directly probes the proposed mechanism—nanocluster segregation driving boundary decohesion—by visualizing and quantifying compositional variations at GBs under service‐like conditions. It is well supported by previous evidence (e.g., PMC6897545::web::008::nanoclustering_induced_gb_embrittlement) and is feasible using advanced characterization methods. However, while highly informative, it may be less immediately actionable for alloy design compared to other routes.

directions.direction: Develop a controlled heat-treatment route to engineer preexisting, grain-boundary–localized Cr-rich precipitates that capture embrittling elements, thereby mitigating nanosegregation at the boundaries.
directions.assessment: This approach offers a direct intervention on the mechanistic pathway by diverting the fast segregation from GBs into engineered precipitates. It respects the constraint of retaining a complex composition and aligns with evidence (e.g., PMC6897545::web::010::gb_segregation_engineering_to_enhance_du, PMC9848264::web::017::discussion). It is practical for further alloy design, though fine-tuning precipitate volume fraction and distribution may be challenging.

directions.direction: Modify the overall composition via minor alloying additions (e.g., suppressor elements) to slow down or inhibit the segregation kinetics of the principal elements to GBs.
directions.assessment: This design strategy attempts to control the intrinsic driving force for nanosegregation by adjusting solute-solvent interactions. Its advantage is that it avoids additional processing; however, the complex thermodynamics in HEAs may mask the effects, and the evidence is less direct on the compositional window for suppressing nanosegregation compared with processing interventions.

directions.direction: Alter the grain boundary morphology through tailored thermomechanical treatments to induce serration, which can distribute strain more evenly and delay the onset of intergranular decohesion.
directions.assessment: Evidence shows serrated grain boundaries enhance ductility by mitigating strain concentration (PMC9848264::web::017::discussion). Although this does not directly eliminate nanosegregation, it provides a way to accommodate its deleterious effects. The physics behind strain distribution is well understood, and the intervention is relatively feasible. Nevertheless, it may only delay brittle failure rather than address the fundamental chemical segregation.

directions.direction: Develop computational models coupling thermodynamic CALPHAD predictions with kinetic segregation simulations to map temperature–time regimes where nanosegregation leads to brittle behavior.
directions.assessment: This approach would provide insight into the parameter space over which GB nanosegregation becomes critical. It respects existing physics and complements experiments, but it relies on accurate input parameters that may be difficult to obtain in such a complex system. It would be more indirect and predictive than a direct mechanical test.

choice.direction: Engineer preexisting Cr-rich grain boundary precipitates via controlled heat treatment to capture the fast-segregating principal elements (Ni, Cr, Mn) and compare against an as-cast single-phase HEA.
choice.why: This route directly intervenes in the hypothesized mechanism responsible for brittleness. Prior evidence suggests that in single-phase HEAs, fast nanoclustering at GBs leads to decohesion and brittle failure at intermediate temperatures, whereas redirecting the segregation into preexisting precipitates can mitigate the ductility loss (see PMC6897545::web::010::gb_segregation_engineering_to_enhance_du and PMC9848264::web::017::discussion). It provides a controlled comparison between conventional-alloy expectations (brittleness from clean single-phase GB nanosegregation) and engineered modifications that capture embrittling elements. This approach is feasible for a strong research group and provides a falsifiable experiment.
